question: Why is there a small balloon near the tip of an indwelling urinary catheter?

options.A: To open up a blocked urethral passage
options.B: To measure the pressure inside the bladder
options.C: To hold the catheter securely inside the bladder
options.D: To prevent bacteria from traveling up the tube

explanation: Great job! Once water goes into that tiny balloon, it acts like an anchor so the tube stays safely put without slipping out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h1)

question: When is using an indwelling catheter most necessary?

options.A: To treat a mild, uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection
options.B: For managing stress incontinence during daytime activities
options.C: As a convenient alternative for an elderly patient who dislikes walking
options.D: For accurate urine output monitoring in a critically ill patient

explanation: Spot on! Catheters carry infection risks, so we save them for serious needs like critical care, surgery, or major retention—not just for convenience. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h1)

question: About how long is the adult female urethra?
explanation: You've got this! The female urethra is quite short (about 4 cm), which makes catheterization quick, though it also means bacteria have a shorter trip to cause trouble. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h2)

question: Oops! During insertion, your catheter accidentally slips into the female vagina. What should you do next?

options.A: Wash the same catheter with antiseptic soap and try again
options.B: Leave it temporarily as a landmark and insert a new sterile catheter
options.C: Push it deeper into the vagina to find the correct opening
options.D: Remove it and immediately push that same tube into the urethral meatus

explanation: Smart nursing move! Leaving that stray tube in the vagina stops you from accidentally making the same mistake twice on your next try. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h2)

question: What does the French (Fr) scale tell you about a urinary catheter?

options.A: The outer diameter of the catheter tube
options.B: The maximum volume of the retention balloon
options.C: The total length of the drainage tubing
options.D: The rigidity of the catheter material

explanation: Think of the French size as the thickness of the tube. The bigger the number, the wider the catheter! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h3)

question: Why would a patient need a triple-lumen catheter for continuous bladder irrigation?

options.A: It increases the French size automatically during surgery
options.B: It provides separate channels for drainage, balloon inflation, and fluid instillation
options.C: It prevents the patient from accidentally pulling the tube out
options.D: It allows three nurses to flush the bladder simultaneously

explanation: Exactly! Three separate pathways mean fluid can flow in, urine can flow out, and the balloon stays inflated all at the same time. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h3)

question: Before opening a standard catheter kit, which major allergies must you always check for?
explanation: Always double-check! Standard kits usually contain latex tubing and iodine cleansers, so catching an allergy early saves your patient a lot of pain. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h4)

question: Why should you check for bladder fullness using a scanner or your hands before placing a catheter?

options.A: To numb the urethral canal before inserting the tube
options.B: To confirm there is an actual need to drain urine before invading sterile tissue
options.C: To measure the exact concentration of bacteria inside the bladder
options.D: To determine what size French catheter is required

explanation: Brilliant! Because catheters bring infection risks, we only want to insert one when we are certain the patient's bladder is actually holding urine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h4)

question: When cleaning the female urethral area with antiseptic swabs, which direction should you wipe?
explanation: Always wipe from cleanest to dirtiest—front to back! This keeps nasty bacteria away from the urinary opening. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h5)

question: Your patient cries out in sharp pain as you inflate the catheter balloon. What is your very first move?

options.A: Stop inflation immediately and check if the catheter is still in the urethra
options.B: Push the catheter in harder to reach the proper depth
options.C: Inject the remaining water quickly to finish the procedure
options.D: Administer an oral painkiller and continue inflating

explanation: Stop right away! Pain during balloon inflation usually means the balloon is stuck inside the narrow urethra instead of resting safely in the bladder. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h5)

question: Where must the urine drainage bag be placed relative to the patient's bladder at all times?

options.A: Resting directly on the patient's chest
options.B: Below the level of the bladder
options.D: Hanging from the top bed rail

explanation: Gravity is your friend here! Keeping the bag lower than the bladder stops urine from flowing backward and causing an infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h6)

question: Why is it important to tape or strap the catheter tubing to the patient's thigh?

options.A: It prevents pulling and friction injuries inside the fragile urethral canal
options.B: It eliminates the need for daily perineal hygiene care
options.C: It speeds up the rate of urine production from the kidneys
options.D: It prevents the drainage bag from filling up too quickly

explanation: Spot on! Securing the tube stops body movements from tugging on it, protecting delicate tissues from painful friction. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h6)

question: What is the single best way to prevent a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)?

options.A: Clamp the catheter for two hours every afternoon
options.B: Remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer medically necessary
options.C: Apply antibiotic ointment around the meatus three times a day
options.D: Disconnect the drainage tubing every morning to flush it out

explanation: You've got it! The golden rule of preventing catheter infections is taking the tube out the moment it's no longer needed. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h7)

question: Why is breaking the seal of a closed urinary drainage system a bad idea?

options.A: It stops urine production in the kidneys
options.B: It causes the retention balloon to deflate spontaneously
options.C: It changes the French size of the catheter tubing
options.D: It allows bacteria to enter the system and travel directly into the bladder

explanation: Keep that system closed! Breaking the seal opens a wide-open highway for germs to march straight up into the bladder. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h7)

question: Your catheterized patient has had no urine output for two hours and feels lower belly discomfort. What do you check first?

options.A: Check the tubing for kinks, twists, or compression under the patient
options.B: Call the doctor to report acute kidney failure
options.C: Remove the catheter immediately and insert a new one
options.D: Inject sterile water into the balloon to secure it further

explanation: Always look for the simple fix first! A twisted or flattened tube is usually the culprit when urine suddenly stops flowing. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h8)

question: What does a nurse suspect when thick blood clots keep blocking a urinary catheter?

options.A: Complete failure of the patient's kidneys to filter blood
options.B: An allergic reaction to the latex material of the drainage bag
options.C: Internal obstruction of the lumen requiring patency check or irrigation
options.D: A normal healing process that requires no nursing intervention

explanation: Clots and debris can clog up the inside of the tube like a blocked drain, meaning you'll need to check if it's patent or flush it. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h8)

question: What crucial step must you never forget before pulling out an indwelling catheter?

options.A: Completely deflate the balloon by withdrawing all the sterile water with a syringe
options.B: Apply heat packs to the patient's lower abdomen
options.C: Clamp the catheter for 24 hours to exercise the bladder
options.D: Disconnect the drainage bag and flush the tube with antiseptic solution

explanation: Never skip this! Pulling out a catheter while the balloon is still full will cause severe, painful injury to the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h9)

question: What is an important thing to monitor after you take out a patient's catheter?

options.A: Insert a new catheter immediately to prevent infection
options.B: Monitor and document the patient's first spontaneous urination within 6 to 8 hours
options.C: Ensure the patient drinks at least five liters of water in the first hour
options.D: Check the patient's blood pressure every fifteen minutes

explanation: You're doing great! Watching for that first pee lets you know the bladder is waking back up and helps catch any post-removal retention early. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h9)
